title: When the Aftermath Wakes
premise: After her mother's funeral, Mara Ishikawa catalogues the house and discovers her family was known in another town by a name no one ever spoke — and that a stranger at the funeral, Daniel Okafor, has spent thirty years waiting for someone to say it aloud. As Mara pieces together letters, ledgers, and a buried settlement, she learns her mother helped conceal an industrial fire that killed four workers, and that the compensation meant for their families was quietly absorbed into the Ishikawa inheritance. Torn between protecting her grieving father and brother, who built their lives on that money, and honoring the victims' surviving kin — including Daniel's dying sister — Mara must decide whether truth can be given without destroying everyone who receives it. In the end she bypasses the courts entirely, returning the estate's core assets to the victims' families through an anonymous trust, accepting that her own inheritance is now only the story, told honestly at last.
about_author: Paloma Nakamura is a former probate paralegal from Vancouver whose decade of handling contested estates taught her how much of a family's history lives inside its paperwork. She writes quiet, morally intricate fiction about the debts we inherit without knowing we've signed for them.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Three days after the funeral, Mara catalogs her mother's belongings room by room, treating grief like an administrative task. She notices small wrongnesses: a locked drawer, a name scratched out of an old address book. Emotional beat: numbness beginning to crack.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. At the memorial reception, a quiet stranger, Daniel Okafor, offers condolences but calls the family by a surname — Verrecchia — that Mara has never heard. Her father goes white and ends the conversation. Beat: first fissure in the official story.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, with brief interludes from her mother's old letters. Searching the locked drawer, Mara finds a bankbook under the other name and a 1994 newspaper clipping about a factory fire in Alder Bay. Beat: curiosity hardening into dread.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Days
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She moves through the week like a renter in her childhood home, watching her father perform composure and her brother Theo deflect with jokes. She says nothing about what she found. Beat: loyalty as a form of silence.

chapters.title: Daniel Okafor Returns
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. He waits outside the house and finally tells Mara plainly: his sister Amara was injured in the Alder Bay fire; the company that owned it was owned, in turn, by the woman they just buried. Beat: the past arrives with a face and a deadline.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Cruelties
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Cross-referencing ledgers, Mara traces payments labeled 'settlements' that stopped abruptly in 1995 — money that should have gone to four families. Beat: the horror of arithmetic; grief becomes evidence.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Jokes
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo privately admits he already suspected something years ago and chose not to look, because the business loan that saved his restaurant came from 'the estate.' Beat: complicity as love, love as excuse.

chapters.title: The Father's Version
chapters.summary: Father Kenji's POV. Kenji tells Mara a softened story: her mother took over her grandfather's debts and liabilities, paid what she could, hid the rest to protect the children. Beat: sympathy complicating judgment; every villain is someone's parent.

chapters.title: Amara's Room
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. Daniel brings Mara to meet his sister Amara, now frail, who remembers the fire with terrible clarity and asks only one thing: not money, but acknowledgment — a record that says their names. Beat: stakes shift from restitution to recognition.

chapters.title: The Fourth Family
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara tracks down the fourth victim's daughter, Ruth Calloway, who took a settlement long ago and signed a silence agreement, and who wants nothing reopened. Beat: the cost of truth made flesh; not all wounds want air.

chapters.title: Lawyers and Ghosts
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A family attorney warns Mara that pursuing this could unravel the estate, expose Theo's business, and leave her father destitute at seventy-eight. Statute limitations shield the company but not the conscience. Beat: the law's limits drawn clearly.

chapters.title: What Mother Meant to Say
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, reading a final unsent letter. Her mother drafted a confession twice and stopped both times, writing 'they will hate me less if I am only dead.' Beat: Mara inherits not guilt but the unfinished sentence.

chapters.title: Theo's Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The restaurant's lender calls in a review; rumors of the family name surface. Theo confronts Mara, accusing her of arson against their own lives. Beat: open rupture between siblings; loyalty and truth stop pretending to be allies.

chapters.title: Kenji Breaks
chapters.summary: Kenji's POV. Confronted with the full ledger, Kenji confesses he knew everything and chose the children over the strangers, and asks Mara — begs her — to let the dead stay dead. Beat: the moral center of the book; the question stated outright.

chapters.title: The Question Arranged Around
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Alone in her mother's study, Mara articulates the family's founding question: can a good life be built knowingly on an unpaid debt? She drafts two plans — one legal, one outside the law. Beat: stillness before decision.

chapters.title: Ruth Changes Her Mind
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth, seeing Amara's condition reported in a local piece, visits her — two survivors across a table — and withdraws her objection, asking instead to be present when names are restored. Beat: solidarity as grace; the coalition forms.

chapters.title: Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. With a discreet estate planner, Mara structures an irrevocable trust transferring the core properties and investments to the four families, bypassing probate and her father's consent. Beat: decisive action; justice as design, not verdict.

chapters.title: The Reckoning at Dinner
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. Mara tells her father and brother together. Kenji weeps without protest; Theo storms out, his livelihood visibly dissolving. Beat: climax — the family arranged around silence finally hears it break.

chapters.title: Amara's Names
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. At a small gathering, Mara reads aloud the four victims' names, the circumstances, and her mother's confession, then hands each family their portion. Amara, too weak to speak, taps the page twice. Beat: catharsis; acknowledgment achieved.

chapters.title: What Theo Keeps
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Weeks later, Theo reopens the restaurant smaller, on his own credit, and comes to the house not to forgive but to help pack. Beat: partial reconciliation; forgiveness left honestly incomplete.

chapters.title: Estate Sale
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The house empties; strangers carry away the furniture of a hidden life. Mara keeps only the address book with the crossed-out name, un-crossed now in her own hand. Beat: lightness after loss; tenancy ends.

chapters.title: When the Aftermath Wakes
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, closing letter to her mother. Mara writes that she is neither owner nor tenant of the past anymore, only its witness, and that waking an aftermath is not destruction but the beginning of repair. Final beat: peace earned, not granted.
